newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ELKINGTON LEADS PLAYERS CHAMPIONSHIP BY TWO STROKES.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELKINGTON LEADS PLAYERS CHAMPIONSHIP BY TWO STROKES.

text.p: Steve
Elkington took a two-stroke lead into the final round of the
Players Championship despite misfiring with bogeys on the last
two holes on Saturday.
The Australian limped in with a third-round 68 at Sawgras
for a 13 under par and a two-stroke margin over Scott Hoch,
who shot a seven-under-par 65.
In third place at eight under par and five strokes off the
lead were Billy Andrade, who had a 68, and Tom Purtzer, with a
69. Only seven players will go into the final round within
seven strokes of Elkington.
"My bogey, bogey finish wasn't what I wanted, but it
didn't upset me because I played so well today," Elkington
said. "I mean, those holes are hard. You can easily bogey
them, and at this point I'm not protecting my lead, I'm just
trying to finish my round."
After 11 holes on Saturday Elkington was six under on the
day and had stretched the tournament lead, which he has held
since Thursday, to five strokes. He birdied the first three
holes for an immediate four-stroke lead, then added three more
birdies through the 11th hole.
"Obviously, if I play well tomorrow, I've probably just
got to beat one guy, or maybe two or three. If I don't play so
well, then I'll bring in more guys. So everyone is hoping that
I won't play well tomorrow, though those guys at six, even,
eight under or whatever will have to shoot a hell of a round
anyway," said Elkington.
Elkington, who has won two of his last three tournaments,
won here in 1991.
Hoch's 65 was the day's low round and his best score at
Sawgrass. Hoch has never played well here, last year was the
first time since 1987 he made the cut. His best finish was a
tie for 13th in 1982.
Hoch was the only player in the field without a bogey on
Saturday.
"I putted very well, although I did have a couple of
birdie opportunities that I didn't give the best effort," Hoch
said.
After his round, Hoch broke a three month boycott off the
print media, begun, he said, because he had been misquoted by
a reporter.
He said he broke the boycott because it was the PGA Tour's
tournament, and he feared he would be fined the amount of his
winnings,
"I'm just kidding, but my purse might be turned over to
charity," Hoch said.
